extracted.intended_audience: PR students and early-career public relations practitioners (students learning to pitch journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for students and early-career PR practitioners on how to research, craft, time, and deliver pitches to journalists (email and phone) to build relationships and earn placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research my audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are unique people with diverse styles, tastes and interests. Before pitching, include a “beat” section in the media list that covered the journalist’s interests, significant prior stories and information from the outlet’s website, if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the beat section to determine if the story is a good fit. Researching recent stories and interests helps tailor the pitch and increases receptivity. Media lists should be dynamic and updated regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media lists are dynamic documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Media lists are dynamic documents that can be updated and revised at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep contacts, beats, past interactions, and outlet preferences current. Treat the media list as a living dossier that informs personalized outreach rather than a static spreadsheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor communication to each journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important lesson was to tailor my communication to each journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-size-fits-all blasts; reference the journalist’s beat, prior work, or outlet needs. Personalized outreach builds trust and shows you’ve done homework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative-style press releases for large markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Most modern journalists working in large markets prefer narrative-style press releases that contain the entire story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative releases read more like a feature and make it easier for busy reporters to pick up the story. Use narrative format especially when pitching larger-market outlets; it increases likelihood of placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain inverted pyramid/short releases for small/local markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-paragraph press releases adhering to the inverted pyramid still have their uses, especially in smaller markets with localized publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, straight-to-the-point releases for local outlets that need quick copy or have simple content requirements. Know the outlet’s preferred style before choosing format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching a complete story and provide contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitching a complete story and providing contact information makes their job easier and increases the likelihood they will pick up a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full story details, quotes, facts, and clear contact info so reporters can act immediately. Make it simple for them to follow up or write directly from the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: best hours to email
rubrics_metrics.description: Most reporters and editors actively check emails from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., with a break at noon for lunch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid emailing too early (will be drowned out) or too late (reporter may be out covering something). Aim for mid-morning to early afternoon windows when inbox attention is higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: best days to pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: The best days I found to pitch were Tuesday through Thursday. Monday is when journalists tend to get the most emails, while Friday is too late in the week for the pitch to be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule pitches mid-week to avoid inbox overcrowding (Monday) and reduced editorial interest (Friday/weekend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Email brevity: less is more
rubrics_metrics.description: When sending pitch emails, I found that less was more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the email short; emphasize the newsworthy elements and significance. The email should aim to grab attention and encourage opening the attached/full release rather than sell the entire story in the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the press release in the email and attach a PDF
rubrics_metrics.description: I would paste the press release directly underneath the email copy and also attach it as a PDF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both inline copy (for quick skimming) and an attachment (for easy saving/printing). This redundancy helps busy reporters access the release in their preferred way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phone pitches are more effective than email
rubrics_metrics.description: Email pitches are far less effective than phone pitches. Of every placement my stories received, only one was directly from an email pitch; the rest were from phone calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize calling when possible to build relationships and get immediate responses. Use calls to create a personal connection; reserve email for follow-up or when phone contact is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Come across as human / be natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Coming across as human is vital; a common perception of PR professionals is that we are pesky and fake, so finding ways to engage with journalists naturally is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sounding robotic or scripted. Use conversational language, show authentic interest in the topic, and treat the interaction as a two-way conversation rather than a hard sell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with an engaging phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead into the pitch with the phrase, 'I have a story I think you might be interested in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind of lead-in signals relevance and invites attention. Combine it with a quick reference to the journalist’s work to demonstrate fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference at least one recent story of the journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Research at least one of their recent stories so I could relate it to my pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning a specific recent piece shows respect for their beat and increases chances they’ll listen. It also informs how you frame the story to fit their coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open calls with a permission question
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the phone call with a question: after introducing myself, I would ask either 'is this a bad time?' or 'do you have a minute?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking for permission lets the journalist set the pace, encourages engagement, and often yields either immediate attention or a callback time. It signals respect for their schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believe in the story and vary your tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to sell someone on a story was to believe in it myself; speaking from the heart and alternating tone made me more engaging than reading a script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be genuinely invested in the pitch; vary cadence and inflection to sound conversational. Scripts can make you sound robotic — use them only as prompts, not read verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat unsuccessful pitches as relationship opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes journalists said they were not interested, but unsuccessful pitches can lead to fruitful conversations and referrals to colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use declines as a chance to learn what the journalist wants, ask for referrals, and keep lines of communication open. Follow up respectfully when appropriate; building relationships matters more than any single placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and acceptance of non-responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many calls went to voicemail and many emails went unanswered, and that was okay. Not every pitch will land where it needs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that outreach has low conversion; maintain persistence and view each outreach as an opportunity to connect rather than guarantee placement. Keep track of responses and callbacks in your media list.
